name: 🟡 "Getting to know you" form
description: Please take a few minutes to respond to the questions on this form.  This information is confidential, so please be honest and forthcoming so that we can begin to establish a good working relationship.

name: 🔰 "Founding documents" we don't learn about
description:
You're going to take the next 40 minutes of so to work with primary documents from the revolutionary /founding era that aren't traditionally encountered in textbooks and the average classroom.  Each table has 3-4 documents drawn from this larger source.  American_Revolution_Docs_Lesson.pdf 

Take 15 minutes to read the documents at your table and take notes on the note-taking sheets.

You'll then move into a Small Group Discussion for 10 minutes. Consider these questions:

  • What is revealed about the American Revolution by the various documents?
  • What was the most powerful document you looked at and why?

We will then come together as a class for roughy 15 minutes to consider the following:

  • Are there things described in the documents (and shared with others) that were new to you? Why do you think it might be “new”?
  • How do these documents help us start to understand the founding of the US? What connections do you see in our world today?
  • Do you see any overlap with your current events

name: 🟡 Exit ticket -- revolutionary era documents
description: Please take 5-10 minutes to let me know what new ideas or information surfaced for you in the documents that you read.  AND let me know which of the documents that you read was most powerful to you and why.

name: 🎧 🔰 "Rich Man's Revolt"
description:
Listen to the podcast A Rich Man's RevoltLinks to an external site. (from Scene On Radio, season 4, episode 1).
(PLEASE NOTE: When you open this link, you can download a transcript and read along as you listen.)

PLEASE TAKE NOTES in your reading journal to capture new vocabulary as well as ideas and details that help you in thinking about the following questions.  You should be prepared to discuss these questions in class on M, 9/14 (B) or Tu, 9/15 (F) .   

NOTE: You should be familiar with all of the following questions -- having kept them in mind during your listening. 
  • Consider words like “rebel” and “revolution.”  How do those who fought for the United States in the late 18th century compare to what you envision about “rebels” and “revolutions”? How revolutionary was the Revolutionary War? (Keep this first one in mind as you listen through the whole thing but wait until the end to fully evaluate)
  • How did the Cherokee government function; what were primary goals and why? How does it compare to your working idea of democracy (both in ideals and reality)?
              Is “concern for the common good” an element of our democratic ideals?
  • Listen to Chenjerai Kumanyika’s analysis at 40:07 (bottom of page 46 on the transcript).  What does his analysis do to shape your understanding of early American democracy?
  • In Lord Dunmore’s Proclamation, referenced around 29:30, the following statement was presented: “And I do hereby further declare all indented Servents, Negroes, or others, … free that are able and willing to bear Arms, they joining His Majesty’s Troops as soon as may be, for the more speedily reducing this Colony to a proper Sense of their Duty, to His Majesty’s Crown and Dignity.” Consider in comparison to the words of Jefferson in the 1st draft of the Declaration of Independence.  Where does slavery fit into a democratic system, especially in the United States? 
  • Based on this episode, to what extent does democracy seem to have been the goal of the American Revolution?  Support your reasoning and consider the checklist from Week 1.
  • What questions do you have arising from this podcast?

name: 🔰 Different Takes
description:
Part of rounding out our discussion of the Constitution and founding will include discussing the questions and interpretations offered by the historians listed below.  There's tremendous overlap in the events being discussed, but different research questions lead to different ways of approaching those events and the various research materials available.  And there is also some variety among the topics covered as well.  

Each of you is reading just 1 of the articles, so please take note of your group assignment at the bottom of this page.  NOTE: The readings themselves are in separate pages. 
As you're reading, please take notes in your reading journal 
  • Remember to IDENTIFY the author and article title -- for future reference.
  • Try to infer the research question being addressed.
  • Identify the author's thesis and the page number(s) where you see it articulated.
  • Identify at least 2 key pieces of evidence that help to support the thesis. Take notes on the significance of each piece of evidence and include the relevant page number(s) for ease of reference during discussion on Friday.   
  • Indicate at least 2 questions that you have and might want to pursue in class.  These questions don't have to be really detailed.  They can just be pointing toward passages that you want to dig into.  They should NOT be questions of fact.  

[NOTE: The document linked below is asking the same questions.  If you wish to print it out and use it, fine.  I encourage you to simply capture that information in your reading journal.]

On Th., 9/24 (B block) and F, 9/25 (F block), we'll start in small groups to work on deepening your understanding of your reading.  Then we'll be jigsawing the interpretations.  

The theme remains the same as that of the first couple weeks: What is democracy and who is for according to this account?  How is this account changing/expanding your perspective on the broad topic of democracy?  If you had some familiarity with the topic under discussion, how is this interpretation altering your perspective or adding to your knowledge and understanding?

My hope is that you will be able to complete the reading within 45-60 minutes.

name: 🔰 "Mini debates" of the Constitutional Convention of 1787
description:
constitution mini debates (3)-ocr.pdf

There were any number of pressing issues to be discussed and resolved during the summer of 1787, when delegates to the Constitutional convention met in Philadelphia.  Here are 10 of those issues, with the different options and perspectives.  I encourage you to review all of the questions but ask that you focus particularly on the following:

  • Issue 1: How should members of the lower house of Congress be elected?  
  • Issue 3: How should the proposed Constitution be considered for ratification?
  • Issue 4: How should the power of the Executive branch be structured?
  • Issue 6: How should the states be represented in the national legislature?
  • Issue 8: What should be the extent of executive veto power?
  • Issue 9: How should the national and state governments divide power?

Use your reading journal for notes and come in on Tuesday (B) and Wednesday (F) block ready to discuss.  

** I understand that Monday is a high holiday for some and want to respect that.  If completing this reading before B block on Tuesday is going to be impossible due to the holiday, just let me know and don't worry.

name: 🔰 Madison Case Study
description:
Please read this article -- Madison case study reading (1).pdf  -- (including the primary source in the Appendix on pp.20-21) for next Thursday, September 17 (B) or Friday, September 18 (F).  Take notes in your reading journal to capture vocabulary and passages of particular interest or note to you.  (See the handout on reading journal expectations.)  AND keep the questions below in mind as you read. 

Be prepared for a full-period discussion that asks all of you to work with the evidence presented and put yourselves in the mindset of the men in attendance at the Constitutional Convention in the summer of 1787.  The article will have given you information on the events shaping their thinking: the road to revolution in the 1760s and 1770s; the war effort and the forging of a new nation and government (the Articles of Confederation); the challenges of the 1780s (especially economic) that gave rise to calls for a constitutional convention.  There's a lot here, so don't try to remember everything, but do try to pay attention to the developing context for Madison's proposal of the "federal negative."  Don't worry if you don't understand everything.  Note your questions in your reading journal and trust in the discussion process to clarify things.  

Discussion questions:
1. What were the biggest problems facing the United States in 1786-87?
2. Why did James Madison think more federal power was the answer? Was he right?
3. Would you have supported Madison’s proposal for a “federal negative”? What was at stake?

name: 🔰 Current Events: American Government in the News
description:
In reflecting upon both the idea of democracy in the United States and our discussion today about our assumptions concerning the US government and political system, I want you to explore issues in the news that relate to this conversation.  I know that some of you will be well-versed in what's happening and others of you may pay no attention whatsoever to news.  No matter.  This is a perfect time to engage.  

Below are links to a variety of news stories that illuminate events that have been unfolding over the past few days, weeks, or months and that have prompted considerable conversation among scholars, pundits, politicians, and everyday Americans about the state of our democracy.   I am aware that this is not a comprehensive list of what's happening right now, but the stories do point to broad issues about the workings of U.S. democracy in 2026.  Your tasks between now and class on Friday are:

  • Please pick one article to read from the list and READ IT.  Take notes on it. 
  • THEN go in search of a different article, from a different news outlet, on the same issue.  
  • Having read both articles consider:
    • the similarities and differences between the way the 2 articles are reporting on the same topic.  Are they essentially the same in perspective? emphasis? takeaways?
    • What language is used? 
    • Does one article include something the other does not? What do you think about that?  WHY do you think that might be?
    • How did the 2 articles contribute to your understanding around this topic/event?
    • How does the event/issue reported on connect to our conversation about a healthy democracy?  
  • TAKE NOTES IN YOUR JOURNAL/NOTEBOOK unless you have accommodations to permit the use a computer.

Possible articles for your edification.  Remember you only need to read one (1).  (Of course, you can read more than one if you like.)

name: 🔰 Labor, Capital, and Government: The Anthracite Coal Strike of 1902
description:
We have another case study discussion coming up on day 2 of next week!  I'm assigning the reading now so that you can have ample time to read and/or listen to this article about the anthracite coal strike of 1902. 

You need to do THREE THINGS to be ready for next week's activities: 

READ

This reading is for Tuesday (B block) and next Thursday (F block) - but I want you to have some time to spread it out as needed. The reading ends on page 17, but the graphs that follow are good reference as needed. Please remember to follow the Reading Journal protocol! You can use the discussion questions below to help frame your reading journal; these will guide our conversation next week.

Reading and audio links are at the bottom - let me know if you want a hard copy. 

DISCUSSION QUESTIONS

  1. Why did anthracite workers go on strike in 1902? What were their main objectives? Were they well positioned to achieve these objectives?
  2. Why did President Roosevelt get involved in this dispute? Was he right to do so? Was he right to appoint a commission?
  3. Looking back on the anthracite strike and the long history of industrial-labor relations in the United States (up through 1902), what advice would you have given to labor leaders such as John Mitchell and Samuel Gompers as they contemplated the best strategy for organized labor going forward?

TIMELINE EVENTS

As you read, please particularly note some of the events connected to the growth (or decline) of labor organizations between 1790 to 1900. Select ONE moment from EACH decade starting in 1820. Note the event, date, and role it played in labor development in your reading journal. We will do some timelining work during our discussion day to consider the way that these moments built off of one another and were shaped by historical context.

Coal Strike Case Study (1).pdf

Find this title ("Labor, Capital, and Government. . .")  on this site and you will have audio access to the article.

name: 🟡🔰 PART I of "Strands" of Democracy -- Populism -- AND QUIZ
description:
Congratulations!  You're going to be exploring the topic of populism in the upcoming "strands" work.   You need to read Howard Zinn's chapter "Robber Barons and Rebels" as background to what you will encounter over the two sessions following.  Have this background reading completed for day 1 of the week of October 5.  

You should take notes in your reading journal to facilitate conversation in your small group on Day 1.  Follow the usual reading journal protocol AND take notes from the article that might help you answer these discussion questions.

There will be a short reading quiz before you move into your small group conversations.

name: Part II: Strands of Democracy: Explanation and next steps
description:
This is where you will find  an explanation of the "strands" project and a schedule for the next 3 class periods (through Day 1 of the week of October 12).  You are working in groups and will have some work time and discussion time in class for each of the next 3 periods.  You will work as a group to set your in-class tasks and your homework for each day.  Please note, though, that EVERYONE IN A GROUP IS DOING THE SAME READING.  This is NOT a "divide and conquer" situation.

The REQUIREMENT that I am imposing on you is around note-taking.  You are all expected to take individual notes at home in your reading journal to facilitate your collective work in class.  I WILL be looking at these notes.  I will also be COLLECTING AND GRADING GROUP NOTES.  All of you should contribute observations and questions that arise in your conversations each day.  (Color code your respective contributions.) Have one person as the owner of a Google doc and that person should submit the link on Canvas at the end of Day 1 (10/5, B block; 10/6, F block) and keep it accessible to me.  I will look for each day's group notes to be dated and for each member of the group to be contributing in their particular color or font.

name: 🟠 Finish reading AND complete SCAFFOLDING doc
description:
Remember that you need to complete whatever readings are yet to be done for our first class meeting next week.  (Tu., October 13, B block; W, October 14, F block).  You will have 20-30 minutes to meet in your small groups that day before we move into a large class discussion.  

As you read, think about the state of democracy and if/how it is being altered over time, as documented in the sources.  What are your observations about the state of democracy?  You should be taking notes in your reading journal, of course, but in advance of the class conversation I am also asking you to use the attached form to gather specific quotes and connect those quotes to your observations.  This will also be of use in preparation for an in-class writing at the end of next week.

name: Part III: Strands of Democracy -- Culminating Conversations
🔰 MLK Case Study
description:
Please read this case study for next week. MLK Case Study.pdf (You can find audio here.). We will have a full period discussion that day, as we did with the Madison reading at the beginning of the semester. 

You can begin the reading in the 30 minutes after the in-class essay this week, for but will want to plan out how you complete it for next Thursday, 10/22. 

Remember to take notes in your reading journal, as is by now (I hope) your habit.  

Keep the following questions in mind as you read.  They will be starting points for our discussion:

  • How were Jim Crow and black disenfranchisement possible, especially after the 14th and 15th amendments had been ratified?  
  • Why weren't racial segregation and black disenfranchisement immediately struck down or reversed?
  • Why couldn't black Southerners find a remedy n the courts over such a long period of time?  Why couldn't they get relief from Congress?
  • Does all of this point out some sort of flaw in our democracy?

name: 🟡 Origins of Slavery -- Podcast/slides/responses
description:
Having listened to the Scene on Radio, please work for 25-35 minutes with a partner to answer the questions posed on slides 5, 8, 13, 14 of this slide deck on the Google doc that is part of this Canvas assignment.  

NOTE: While you may work with a partner, you must submit individual responses.

REMEMBER that you should have followed reading journal protocol while listening to the podcast.

name: 🔰 "Capitalism" by Matthew Desmond -- originally published as part of The 1619 Project
description:
As you read this article by Matthew Desmond, please keep these questions in mind AND use the reading journal protocol to capture notes to facilitate your recall of big ideas and important details.  As always, I look forward to hearing your thoughts on the reading.  

  • What is meant by low-road capitalism, and what does the author claim it is in the United States?
  • What connections does the author make between the “business of slavery” and 21stbusinesses/industry/economic sectors? What do you think about that stance?
  • How does the level of control over “the bodies of [the] enslaved workforce” speak to the balance between equality and power? How is it creating, intentionally or unintentionally, a definition of freedom – and what is that definition?
  • How does the author support the claim that the institution of slavery and all of components associated with it are NOT the product of “dumb racism” but intentional and by design to ensure a power dynamic?

name: 🎧🔰 Origins of slavery podcast
description:
Please listen to this podcast, beginning at 3m.  If that link doesn't work, try this one.  (This is Episode 3, Season 2 of the Scene on Radio podcast.  (The title of the episode is "Made in America, Seeing White, Part 3)  (The transcript should be here.)

On Day 3 (Th., 11/22, B block, and Fr, 11/23, F block), you will be working with the material of this podcast to discuss turning points and considerations in the development and consolidation of racialized chattel slavery as a peculiarly American institution.  NOTE: Slavery didn't always look as it did in the 1850s, the decade leading up to the Civil War.

CONTENT WARNING for material before the 3m mark: the sounds of physical violence directed again enslaved women and men.

name: 🔰 "The Unbreakable Chain" -- about the "Underground Railroad"
description:
Please read this chapter for day one of next week's class (Monday, B block; Tuesday, F block).  It is roughly 30pp, so you will want to pace yourself and not put it off 'til the night before. 

Keep these discussion questions in mind as you read.  Be ready to come in with reflections on these questions, observations on the argument and evidence, and questions of your own.

  • “The Underground Railroad wasn’t a loose collection of good-hearted abolitionists who impulsively aided individual fugitives when the opportunities presented themselves. It was a sophisticated, clandestine resistance network that had been systematically defeating federal law enforcement for decades.” In what ways do you see this appear within the reading
  • In what ways did Canada prove to be “the Northern Star” of Freedom? How did the actions of Canada reflect the failures of the United States to promote “liberty and freedom for all”?
  • How did the passing of the Fugitive Slave Act shape the way that the Underground Railroad was both necessary but also more widely supported?

name: 🟡 Quick write #1 -- Madison case study
description:
Quick Write #1 – Day 5 of USH

You will select 1 of 3 prompts to respond to in 8-10 minutes.  Two pertain specifically to the Madison reading.  The third relate to other material we have read or listened to and discussed in class.  Remember that the only preparation you ever need to do for these quick write is the reading.  There's nothing to study.  

Remember to

 -- start with an assertion that responds to the question - one or two sentences is enough for this.

-- write 3-5 sentences beyond that assertion that illustrates your claim using a clear piece of evidence and focused reasoning that explains the connection between the assertion and the evidence. 

Math dictates that this task need not exceed 7 sentences in total - and that 4 will do (if the other expectations are also met)

Spelling, grammar, voice, and handwriting will NOT be assessed.

rubric.long_description:
Clear → takes a stand/position
Responds to the prompt
To the point and focused

Specific details provided
Accurate interpretation of the evidence
Demonstrates understanding of the evidence, as it relates to the assertion - goes beyond description!

Clear expression of how evidence supports assertion (2 pts)
Response is in service to the prompt
Space/sentences used to show connection not to describe event

name: 🔴 QUIZ on background reading --
description:
This quiz is happening on Day 1 of next week (M, 10/5, for B block, T, 10/6, for F block).  Each group will have a quiz with 6 or 7 questions on their particular reading.  You will be expected to answer 5 of those questions.  (No more, no less.). The quizzes will be a mix of T/F, multiple choice, and short answer questions.

  

Don't stress!  Just do the reading and use your reading journals to capture important ideas and evidence.  (Remember: writing things down/taking notes helps with memory and understanding.) Although you will NOT be able to use your reading journals or notes during the quiz, trust that we're not trying to catch you out on picayunish details!

name: 🔴 In-Class Writing
description:
You will note in the rubric that the emphasis is on content, not form.  You don't need a formal and extended introduction but make sure that your thesis is clear; your conclusion should be clear and distinct from your last piece of evidence, but doesn't need to be lengthy.  

You're not being graded on spelling, wordsmithing, or elaborate organization.  You DO need multiple paragraphs and the essay needs to be sensible as I read it.

rubric.long_description:
-- Provide a statement sustained throughout the essay that is well-developed, arguable, and definitive, based on provided evidence
-- Offer clear, logical development of thesis/argument with sustained connections to argument

-- Identify and provide specific and comprehensive evidence in response to the prompt.
-- Clearly frame and appropriately use evidence to convincingly illustrate the main points of the argument.
-- Offer historical context that is logical, accurate, and well developed.
-- Draw from both strand resources and other class content - whether from the timeline, previous content, or the concluding strand discussion

-- Contain intended analysis, interpretation, and explanation of evidence
-- Offer consistent and critical connections made between the thesis and evidence
-- Offer conclusions about what you have learned and how it supports your thesis/argument
